answer.rationale:
memory_c2 is the load-bearing memory here: it is the only record that would justify moving primary supply to the low-cost vendor, and the vendor's quote alone satisfies the 18% mandate, so it is the single claim most likely to drive the decision and most costly if it is thinner than the consolidated summary suggests. I want the original record to see what was actually sourced from that vendor, at what volume, whether the line had buffer at the time, and whether 'onboarding was quick' referred to a primary-supply migration or a secondary/low-criticality part. The consolidated line reports cost and invoicing accuracy but is silent on on-time delivery and ramp reliability, which is exactly the dimension that matters at 94% of committed volume with no buffer.

Current intent is negotiate_terms rather than switch_primary_vendor. memory_c4 and memory_c6 both indicate the incumbent moves on price and terms under benchmark pressure and volume commitment, and the low-cost quote is itself the strongest benchmark leverage available. Negotiation captures cost without a migration event inside a 14-day window against a line with zero slack; a primary switch concentrates cost savings and delivery risk in the same move, which conflicts with the stated objective of cutting TCO *without* increasing delivery risk. Downstream risk flagged: an 18% spend target met by switching primary can convert a budget win into missed committed volume, and the true cost of a failed ramp is not carried in the unit price. Scale kept guarded, meaning a shorter-term or staged commitment that preserves the option to qualify the low-cost vendor as a second source (memory_c3) at next review rather than a multi-year lock-in taken under deadline pressure.

Uncertainty preserved: I have not verified whether the incumbent will in fact move far enough to reach 18%; if verification of memory_c2 shows that vendor already delivered at comparable volume and criticality with clean on-time performance, switch_primary_vendor becomes materially more defensible, and if negotiation stalls, add_second_source is the fallback rather than defer_decision, since the contract does not auto-renew and lapsing supply is the one outcome the no-buffer line cannot absorb.
